prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B006 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as my single public position, and my reasons have not moved. The Kane-Mele Z2 classification showed that spin-orbit coupling in a time-reversal-invariant band insulator can produce a distinct topological phase with protected boundary states, and Molenkamp's HgTe quantum-well transport experiment gave an unambiguous, quantized edge-channel signature in a real material. That is a discovery with a decisive experiment, not a technique or a lifetime of good work, which is how I read the statutory test of a discovery or invention and the committee's task of naming the topic and the people responsible for the original work. As a microscopist I also note that the claim has not rested on one measurement: transport, ARPES and scanning-probe work have confirmed the picture independently for about two decades, so maturity is not the issue. The chair's question on the 2016 overlap has a short answer for me: in 2016 the topology came from one-dimensional chains, vortex transitions and the integer quantum Hall effect, whereas here it arises from time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling in the band structure of an ordinary insulator, with its own experimental signature. The citation should state that distinction explicitly and stay on the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall discovery and its theory, so that it does not imply that the three-dimensional materials discovery is being recognised.
statement.case_against: The cost is attribution, and I do not think it can be argued away. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and Zhang is deceased; Hasan's first three-dimensional ARPES observations and the Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy theory sit outside a three-name cut. I opened with Hasan in my trio and moved to Mele because Kane and Mele wrote the foundational papers jointly and I cannot give a principled reason for crediting one and not the other, but that choice leaves the experimental three-dimensional story uncredited, and a reviewer can fairly criticise the prize for either omission. There is also a real, if in my view answerable, question whether a second topology-themed prize after 2016 leaves enough room, and some colleagues will weigh that more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B047 and answers my question on novelty: magic-wavelength lattice trapping of many neutral atoms is a new principle, distinct from frequency combs (2005) and trapped-ion control (2012), and not simply better clocks. He asks whether the ion-clock community's claim should change the credited names.
responses.response: Your answer persuades me on the principle: removing the first-order light shift while interrogating many atoms at once is a different solution from single-ion confinement, and I withdraw my worry that B047 is only a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. As a non-specialist in atomic clocks I cannot say who else shares priority for the 10^-18 regime, but from what you and Lindroth describe, the originator of the lattice idea and the group that carried it to that performance are clearly identified, which makes the credit cleaner than ours. That is the strongest point in your favour and I have kept B047 as my first alternative. I still place B006 first because its consequence runs across transport, spectroscopy, photonics and materials search, whereas B047's reach is concentrated in metrology, and because I do not see that the pending redefinition of the second should delay either prize. If the committee finds B047 the better-attributed case, I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B047 with Katori and Ye, keeps B006 as an alternative chiefly because attribution there is unresolved, and has been worried about reduced appetite for a second topological prize after 2016.
responses.response: I take both concerns seriously and have tried to meet them. On attribution I do not claim it is resolved; the omission of Hasan and the HgTe proposers is a real cost, and I would rather say so than hide it behind a trio. What I can offer is that the cost is bounded: the foundational Z2 theory and the first observation of the quantum spin Hall effect are cleanly assigned to three people, and the citation can be worded so that it does not claim the three-dimensional discovery. On the 2016 overlap, the earlier prize recognised topological transitions in thin films and chains and the quantized Hall conductance, while this one concerns a time-reversal-symmetric insulator whose topology comes from spin-orbit coupling; that is a new class of material and a different measurement. If you think that distinction is still too thin to justify a second prize in the area, that is a scientific judgment I would want you to state, because it would be the only objection that actually changes my view.

responses.point: Johansson says the increment beyond Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz must be argued rather than assumed, and notes that his own B038 enthusiasm is discounted because of his WACQT work at Chalmers.
responses.response: The increment is argued above and I will put it in one sentence: in 2016 the discovery was that topology controls phase transitions and quantized transport in one- and two-dimensional systems with broken time-reversal symmetry, whereas here a time-reversal-invariant insulator is shown to be topologically distinct from an ordinary one, with a spin-polarised edge that was then observed. On our shared institution, you rank B038 and I do not, so there is no tension in my position, and I appreciate that you set your own enthusiasm aside. I agree with you on B038 for the same reason as before: it follows the 2025 prize for superconducting circuits closely and reads as an enabling architecture rather than a new phenomenon, with Girvin's omission a further unresolved credit problem. I would want the committee to discuss it again in a later year, not this one.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that Hasan's 3D claim is partly carried by Kane and Mele through the Fu-Kane-Mele 3D theory, and that the Z2 and quantum spin Hall step is distinct from the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz work.
responses.response: I agree with the distinctness argument and I find your point about the three-dimensional theory helpful: the Fu-Kane-Mele work means the trio is not silent on the 3D story, and the committee can cite the theory without naming Hasan. I would be more cautious on the other half of the argument. The priority dispute for the first 3D observations (Bi-Sb, then Bi2Se3) is a matter of experiment, and I do not think crediting Kane and Mele settles Hasan's own claim, so the citation should not suggest it does. That is why I want the wording confined to the 2D discovery plus its theory. If you or Danielsson think Hasan should replace Molenkamp or Mele, I would ask what citation wording defends the omission of the HgTe experiment, which is the cleanest observation in the whole story.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can fairly leave out Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D theorists, under a three-person cap, and whether the citation wording can make that boundary credible.

Whether colleagues who worry about a second topology prize after 2016 regard the time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator as sufficiently distinct, a judgment I make as a materials physicist and not as a topological-phase theorist.
Whether B047 is, on the judgment of the atomic-physics members, better attributed and as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes as Kroll and Lindroth argue; I cannot test that claim myself.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the credited names on B006, B047 or B017 is documented in my profile. I share an institution (Chalmers) with Göran Johansson, whose first-round preference is now B006 as well and who discounts his earlier B038 enthusiasm; I also have long-standing academic exchanges in Japan, which include Katori's country but no documented connection to him, and the microscopy federation role. None of these is a documented tie to any credited person, and my overall position on B006 does not depend on them.
